..
KEY MESSAGE 1...
Strong shear and instability will continue to support the
potential for severe thunderstorms across portions of the area
through this evening. The 18Z special PIT sounding shows ML CAPE
around 3200 j/kg, with effective shear of 30-40kt. DCAPE values
were around 1000 j/kg, indicating a damaging wind potential.
Large hail will also be possible with the amount of buoyancy in
place. 

KEY MESSAGE 2... 
Strong 594 dam ridging remains centered across the Southeast 
with the axis of the ridge extended north through the Plains. 
Locally, we're parked beneath west-northwest mid- level flow, 
and subtle impulses in the flow combined with mesoscale surface 
features will continue to be the driver of our thunderstorm 
complexes over the next 48 hours.

For the rest of Wednesday, expect that we'll be mostly dry into the 
early afternoon hours with localized subsidence in the wake of 
morning convection. By late afternoon and evening, we should see 
reinvigoration of showers and storms possibly driven by two 
features. The first will be a subtle surface trough and weak mid-
level wave tracking through southern Michigan and eventually over 
Lake Erie. Putting stock in current CAMs is tough, especially as 
they continue to struggle even with ongoing convection, but their 
consensus to fire storms off of that feature combined with a lake 
breeze will likely be one focus. The other is likely to be a density 
gradient along the outflow/cirrus shield from the morning 
convection. It has sagged south toward Pittsburgh late this 
morning, but expectation is it will shift a bit back farther 
northeast as southwesterly flow establishes. CAMs aren't excited
about development along it, but struggle to believe that that's
really going to be the case. The environment will be potent; 
modifying our morning sounding in untapped air suggests dew 
points with a floor in the mid 70s and afternoon highs in the 
upper 80s to low 90s. A belt of 40-50 knot 500 mb flow will 
support effective shear of 30-40 knots and MLCAPE values >3000 
J/kg and steep, nearly dry adiabatic mid-level lapse rates. Any 
storm that develops will have a severe threat. Again, think 
coverage will be highest north and east of Pittsburgh with most 
likely timing from 4pm-midnight.

Confidence in future storm complex progression decreases with time 
in this setup as it's highly dependent on poorly modeled preceding 
rounds, but Thursday looks more favorable to see more widespread 
coverage of storms. The mid-level ridge axis will amplify a bit more 
and gradually slide east which will reorient the mid-level flow more 
northwesterly such that we're better in the path of impulses and 
resultant MCSs. The question is when we get the most coverage. Some 
solutions suggest morning convection again similar to Wednesday 
morning while others don't and hold off until the afternoon. The 
latter case would result in more widespread, severe storms in a 
favorable environment with a 70+% probability of 1000 J/kg SBCAPE 
and 30 knots of shear. If storms do move through in the morning, 
they will carry a severe risk with them as well, there will just be 
more question about threats and whether or not they're surface-
based. Then the waters will become muddier for the afternoon, so we 
just have to take this setup 12-24 hours at a time.

Come Friday, a cold front that's been meandering well off to our 
north finally gets a push to move through and will put an end to the 
unsettled pattern for the weekend. More storms are possible in the 
morning hours ahead of the front, but we should see a cessation from 
north to south in the second half of the day as the front passes 
through. It'll be very timing dependent, but there is a scenario in 
which most of our activity is done by mid-afternoon. Others suggest 
it lingers a bit, especially south of Pittsburgh, into the evening 
hours. The severe outlook for Friday has appropriately been pulled 
south and only left our area south of Pittsburgh in a marginal risk.

KEY MESSAGE 3... 
Aside from the storms, unseasonably warm conditions continue 
through the end of the week with the hottest days being 
Wednesday and Thursday. Heat risk will remain in the major 
category with pockets of extreme in the valleys and urban areas 
where temperatures reach the low to mid 90s and dew points in 
the 70s resulting in heat indices exceeding 100F. Overnight lows
Wednesday night will only dip into the low 70s. Thus, the Heat 
Advisory remains in effect through Thursday.

Have some lower confidence that Advisory criteria will be 
reached widespread on Thursday if convection is more widespread 
in coverage, but with how much uncertainty there is, will let 
the headlines ride as is as areas without convective 
contamination will heat up efficiently.
